title: From Capriasca to the Espigón: the Cap Factory, the Antisonnets, and the Sea at Mar del Plata
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Capriasca, San Juan, Rosario: the House That Kept Failing

stops.name: Sala Capriasca, the birth above the lake
stops.date_confidence: Sources split on the date. The Centro Virtual Cervantes chronology gives 29 May 1892 at seven in the morning; English Wikipedia states 22 May 1892 flatly; Spanish Wikipedia carries 22 May among otras versiones, alongside a version placing the birth aboard a ship at sea. The explanation sometimes offered, that the 29th was a registration date, is unsourced. 29 May follows CVC and the main Spanish Wikipedia text; the contradiction is not resolved here.
stops.campa: At seven in the morning, in a house at Sala Capriasca in the valley above Lugano, Paulina Martignoni bears a daughter to Alfonso Storni. The two married at Origlio in October 1886 and went out to San Juan in Argentina, where Alfonso's brothers build, make soda water and ice, and brew beer; they have come back to Ticino on a doctor's advice. The child is registered Alfonsina. She will have four years in this valley. Two dates for the birth survive in the record, and neither of them has driven the other out.
suggested_refs: The parish and civil registers of Sala Capriasca, Canton Ticino, for the entry of 29 May 1892

stops.name: San Juan, the brewery of the Storni brothers
stops.date_confidence: Attested to August 1896 by CVC for the arrival and to February 1897 for the kindergarten; no days are given and the day here is defaulted. The embarkation at Genoa is attested in the same chronology and is folded into this stop rather than pinned separately.
stops.campa: The family sails from Genoa and lands in Argentina in August, six years after leaving it. Alfonso's brothers had come out to San Juan in 1883 into a concern that builds, makes soda water and ice, and sells the beer they call Cerveza Los Alpes de Storni y Cía. Alfonsina is four and speaks the Italian of the valley. In February of the following year she is put into the kindergarten attached to the San Juan normal school, where for three years she recites, sings, dances, and takes small parts in plays. A brother, Hildo Alberto, is born in August 1898.
suggested_refs: The Cerveza Los Alpes works of Storni y Cía at San Juan, founded by the emigrant brothers in the 1880s
sources: San Juan al Mundo, local history of the Storni brothers' concern

stops.name: Rosario, the café by the Sunchales station
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC gives August 1900 for the move to Rosario and April 1901 for the end of her regular schooling, with no days. The auction of the café repeated in later biography is not in CVC's wording. Coordinates are for central Rosario near the old Sunchales station approach; the exact site of the café is not documented in any source consulted.
stops.campa: The San Juan business is ruined and in August the household comes down to Rosario. Alfonso opens a café near the Sunchales railway station and it does not hold. In April, at nine years old, Alfonsina stops going to school; her mother opens a private school inside the house instead, and teaches there. The girl works: plates in the café, washing, sewing, whatever the school in the front room needs done. What she read in that year, and whether anybody gave her anything to read, the chronology does not say.
suggested_refs: The Sunchales station district of Rosario, c. 1900, and the small commerce that grew along the rail approach

stops.name: Café Suizo, Mendoza and Constitución: the second failure
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC gives July 1902 and a duration of about three months; Spanish Wikipedia supplies the address, Mendoza 3699 at the corner of Constitución. Coordinates geocoded to that address, in the barrio of Echesortu. Accounts placing the café near Rosario's Estación Central are not supported by either source.
stops.campa: Alfonso tries once more: an almacén and café out in Echesortu, at Mendoza 3699 on the corner of Constitución. He calls it the Café Suizo, after a country his daughter cannot remember and has not seen since she was four. Alfonsina waits the tables and washes the glasses in the back. The place lasts about three months and shuts. She is ten years old and has watched her father lose two businesses in two years. Later accounts put this café down by the central station; the address puts it three kilometres out, in a barrio of low houses.
suggested_refs: Mendoza 3699 esq. Constitución, Rosario, the address of the Almacén Café Suizo

stops.name: Rosario, the father dead and the cap factory
stops.date_confidence: Attested to August 1906 by CVC for both the death of Alfonso Storni and the start of the factory apprenticeship; no day is given. Coordinates are the general Rosario pin: the factory is not located in any source consulted.
stops.campa: In August her father dies. Alfonsina is fourteen. Her schooling stopped at nine, and a kindergarten in San Juan and her mother's front-room school are the whole of it. She goes into a cap and hat factory as an apprentice. No source consulted keeps the factory's name or the street it stood on. Every wage she is paid goes straight into the house, which from this month runs on the earnings of a fourteen-year-old and whatever the private school still brings in.
suggested_refs: The cap and hat trade of Rosario in the 1900s, and the apprenticeship of girls into it

segments.name: The Touring Company and the Rural Diploma

stops.name: Tucumán, five months on the road with Tallaví
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC dates the tour with the Spanish actor José Tallaví from March to August 1908, and places the Easter role of San Juan Evangelista at Rosario in 1907. Tucumán stands here for the whole circuit; the individual venues and dates in each province are not documented. A retold story that a stage scandal drove her to a suicide attempt on this tour appears in later biography and is not in the institutional chronology.
stops.campa: At Easter 1907 she plays San Juan Evangelista in a Rosario production. In March of the following year she leaves with the touring company of the Spanish actor José Tallaví and goes out on the road through Santa Fe, Córdoba, Mendoza, Santiago del Estero, and Tucumán, in works of Ibsen, Pérez Galdós, and Florencio Sánchez. She is sixteen. For five months her address is whatever theatre the company has booked, and her trade is standing in front of provincial audiences saying other people's lines out loud.
suggested_refs: The provincial touring circuit of José Tallaví's company, 1908
Florencio Sánchez's repertory as played in the Argentine interior

stops.name: Bustinza, back to her mother's house
stops.date_confidence: Attested to August 1908 by CVC; no day is given. Coordinates from Nominatim for Bustinza, Santa Fe; an earlier working coordinate for this stop fell some 29 km south of the town and is discarded.
stops.campa: In August she leaves the company and goes to Bustinza, a town in departamento Iriondo, out on the grain plain west of Rosario, where her mother is now living. She is sixteen, with no diploma and no trade past the cap factory. Five months on the road have taught her breath, carrying voice, and the timing of a line, and Bustinza is a few streets of a place with nothing to use any of that on. Her mother's house needs her to be useful in it. She stays.
suggested_refs: Bustinza, departamento Iriondo, Santa Fe, and the rural towns of the Rosario grain belt

stops.name: Coronda, the celadora at the rural normal school
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC gives 1909 for the entry into the Escuela Normal Mixta de Maestros Rurales at Coronda and the end of 1910 for the diploma. No days or months are given; March is the ordinary start of the Argentine school year and the day is defaulted.
stops.campa: The mixed normal school for rural teachers at Coronda has only just been created and is taking its first students in the year she arrives. Its director, Mercedes Gervasoni, admits Alfonsina without a completed primary record, on what grounds the chronology does not explain. She pays her way as a celadora, a monitor set over the other students, for something like forty pesos a month, and studies for the certificate that will let her teach in the countryside. At the end of 1910 she takes the diploma of rural teacher.
suggested_refs: The Escuela Normal Mixta de Maestros Rurales at Coronda, founded 1909, and its first cohorts

stops.name: Rosario, Escuela Elemental No. 65
stops.date_confidence: Attested to February 1911 by CVC for the teaching post and the beginning of publication in local magazines; no day is given. The pregnancy is attested by CVC only through her departure for Buenos Aires in January 1912.
stops.campa: Certified, she comes back to Rosario in February and takes a post at Escuela Elemental No. 65, on the strength of a diploma two months old. She begins publishing poems in the local magazines and moves in a literary and political circle that includes Carlos Tercero Arguimbau. She is nineteen, she is teaching, and for the first time in her life she is paid for something she chose. Within the year she is pregnant. In January she is on a train to Buenos Aires.
suggested_refs: The Rosario literary magazines of 1911 that printed her first verse

segments.name: Buenos Aires: the Arrival, the Child, the Desk

stops.name: Retiro, arriving with Darío in her bag
stops.date_confidence: Attested to January 1912 by CVC, which gives no day. The arrival station is inferred: Retiro was the ordinary Buenos Aires terminus of the Rosario line, and no source consulted names where she got off.
stops.campa: In January she leaves Rosario for Buenos Aires, pregnant and unwilling to be looked at by a provincial town for the months it will take. She knows nobody in the city and the city knows nothing about her, which is the point of coming. The Rosario line ends at Retiro, though no source consulted names the platform she got down on, or the hour, or who if anyone was waiting. What she carries off that train is very little money, a sheaf of her own poems, and books by Rubén Darío.
suggested_refs: The Rosario to Buenos Aires line and Retiro terminus, 1912

stops.name: Hospital San Roque, the birth of Alejandro
stops.date_confidence: The date is attested in CVC. The hospital is named only by a 2002 SEPA Argentina interview with Alejandro Storni, not by CVC; coordinates are those of the Hospital Ramos Mejía at Gral. Urquiza 609, Balvanera, the former San Roque. An earlier working coordinate for this stop fell 2 km away in Monserrat and is discarded.
stops.campa: On the twenty-first of April her son is born and registered Alejandro Alfonso Storni. She is nineteen, unmarried, three months into a city of a million and a half strangers, and she raises him herself, on a teacher's certificate and whatever else she can find. She names no father, then or afterward. In 2002 Alejandro, an old man, sits down to be interviewed about his mother; the interview is the only source that says which hospital this was, and he is asked the other question and does not answer it either.
suggested_refs: The Hospital San Roque, later Ramos Mejía, Gral. Urquiza 609, Buenos Aires
SEPA Argentina, 2002 interview with Alejandro Storni
sources: SEPA Argentina, interview with Alejandro Storni (2002)

stops.name: Freixas Hermanos, Bartolomé Mitre 1411: the correspondent
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC gives the year, the firm, the trade in olive oil, and the address. The count of roughly a hundred applicants and the wage comparison of two hundred pesos against a male predecessor's four hundred come through later biography rather than payroll records and are reconstruction. Coordinates geocoded to Bartolomé Mitre 1411; day and month defaulted.
stops.campa: She sits a written examination and is taken on by the olive oil importers Freixas Hermanos on Bartolomé Mitre, with the title of corresponsal psicológico: the one who writes the letters that have to persuade. Later accounts say she was the only woman among some hundred applicants, and that she drew two hundred pesos a month where the man before her in the chair had drawn four hundred. The desk feeds the child and pays the rent. The poems get written in whatever part of the night is left over after both.
suggested_refs: Bartolomé Mitre 1411, Buenos Aires, offices of the importers Freixas Hermanos

stops.name: Buenos Aires, La inquietud del rosal
stops.date_confidence: Attested to March 1916 by CVC, which names the prologue by Juan Julián Lastra; no day is given. The quoted quatrain was read off the digitized first edition. Correction to the imprint carried from that copy: the publisher is Librería La Facultad, Juan Roldán editor, not 'Librería de la Facultad'. Coordinates are the generic Buenos Aires pin, the printing house not being located.
stops.campa: Her first book is printed in March: La inquietud del rosal, with a prologue by Juan Julián Lastra dated autumn of 1915. Storni is twenty-three, a clerk at an oil importer's and the mother of a small boy. One poem in it is dedicated to a dead friend named only by three initials, and it is the poem the country keeps: a woman says she is like the she-wolf, that she broke with the flock and went up the mountain because the flatland tired her. On page 89 the quotation marks open on that quatrain and do not close again for two more pages.
stops.quote: «Yo soy como la loba. / Quebré con el rebaño / Y me fuí a la montaña / Fatigada del llano.
stops.quote_source: La loba, in La inquietud del rosal (Buenos Aires: Librería La Facultad, Juan Roldán editor, 1916), p. 89, from the digitized first edition; the printed quatrain opens with a guillemet that does not close until p. 91.
suggested_refs: La inquietud del rosal (1916), first edition, with Lastra's prologue
sources: La inquietud del rosal (1916), digitized first edition, archive.org 'stornilainquietuddelrosal'

segments.name: The Prize, the Table, and the Woman They Wanted White

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the poem against the war
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC records that the poem appeared once only, in La Acción, the Socialist Party paper, on 6 May 1916, and quotes its opening. The original issue of La Acción was not located. Coordinates are the generic Buenos Aires pin; the paper's offices are not located.
stops.campa: Two months after her first book she publishes a poem in La Acción, the paper of the Socialist Party: a protest against the European war, addressed to the children it has killed. It runs once and is never collected. Europe is in its second year of trenches and Argentina is neutral. The woman writing is a clerk with a four-year-old son, and what she writes is a summons: Christ is told to come down off the wood and walk out into the fields where the blood is setting.
stops.quote: ¡Jesús, Jesús, Jesús, desciende del madero / Y ven hasta la tierra, esclavo del martirio
stops.quote_source: Por los niños que han muerto, La Acción, 6 May 1916, quoted in the Centro Virtual Cervantes chronology; the exclamation opened here does not close until the word obrero, two lines further on.
suggested_refs: La Acción, organ of the Argentine Socialist Party, issue of 6 May 1916

stops.name: Restaurante Génova, the Nosotros dinner
stops.date_confidence: Attested to 9 May 1916 by CVC, which names the venue at Corrientes and Montevideo, the honorand Manuel Gálvez, and the writers present. Coordinates are approximate to that intersection. The Coronado review is quoted by CVC from Nosotros no. 83 without a day; the original issue was not located.
stops.campa: Three days later she goes to a dinner the magazine Nosotros gives at the Restaurante Génova, at Corrientes and Montevideo, in honor of Manuel Gálvez. Roberto Giusti is there, and Alfredo Bianchi, and José Ingenieros, and Alberto Gerchunoff. She is twenty-three, up from Rosario, with one book out and no seat of honor. That same season Nosotros prints Nicolás Coronado on the book: a young poet who has not yet reached the whole of her qualities, but who will give the language more than one valuable thing in future.
stops.quote: En definitiva... es el libro de un poeta joven y que no ha logrado todavía la integridad de sus cualidades, pero que en lo futuro ha de darnos más de una valiosa producción literaria
stops.quote_source: Nicolás Coronado, review of La inquietud del rosal, Nosotros no. 83 (1916), quoted in the Centro Virtual Cervantes chronology
suggested_refs: Nosotros, the review of Giusti and Bianchi, and its dinners of the 1910s

stops.name: Teatro Coliseo, the prize under a false name
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC gives 30 November 1916 for the prize at the ninth Fiesta del Libro, the sum of 655.55 pesos put up by the Jockey Club, the pseudonym Piéridas, and 12 June 1917 for the homage at the Teatro Minerva in Flores. The Minerva event is folded into this stop for want of a documented address; its coordinates were never established.
stops.campa: At the ninth Fiesta del Libro, held in the Teatro Coliseo, the first prize for poetry goes to a submission signed Piéridas: Canto a los niños, six hundred and fifty-five pesos and fifty-five centavos, the money put up by the Jockey Club. The pseudonym is hers. She is still at the importer's desk every morning. Seven months later, out in Flores, the Teatro Minerva holds a public homage in her name; the chronology gives the date of it and no address, and the building cannot now be placed on a map. She is twenty-five.
suggested_refs: The ninth Fiesta del Libro, Teatro Coliseo, November 1916
The Teatro Minerva, Flores, and its June 1917 homage

stops.name: Buenos Aires, El dulce daño
stops.date_confidence: Attested to April 1918 by CVC; no day is given. The quotation was read off the digitized first edition, whose imprint reads Sociedad Cooperativa Editorial Limitada, Avenida de Mayo 791. Coordinates are the generic Buenos Aires pin. The teaching post at the Colegio Marcos Paz is attested by CVC to June 1917.
stops.campa: The second book comes out in April. Its best known poem answers a man who wants her white, wants her of foam and of mother of pearl, a lily chaste above all the others. What that whiteness costs, and who is expected to have paid it, is the whole subject of the poem and of the argument it starts. She has been teaching at the Colegio Marcos Paz since June of the year before, and she still keeps the desk at Freixas Hermanos. The book is read, then and for a century afterward, as love poetry.
stops.quote: Tú me quieres alba, / Me quieres de espumas, / Me quieres de nácar. / Que sea azucena / Sobre todas, casta.
stops.quote_source: Tú me quieres blanca, in El dulce daño (Buenos Aires: Sociedad Cooperativa Editorial Limitada, 1918), p. 103, from the digitized first edition
suggested_refs: El dulce daño (1918), first edition, Avenida de Mayo 791
sources: El dulce daño (1918), digitized first edition, archive.org 'stornieldulcedano'

segments.name: The Citizenship Year and the Years of Exhaustion

stops.name: Montevideo, the lecture on Delmira Agustini
stops.date_confidence: CVC places the Montevideo lecture on Delmira Agustini, and her readings of her own Spanish versions of Delfina Bunge de Gálvez's French poems, in January 1919, with no day. The venue is not named in any source consulted; the coordinates are the Universidad de la República, used as an approximation and not as an attested address.
stops.campa: She crosses the river to Montevideo to lecture on Delmira Agustini, the Uruguayan poet five years dead, and to read her own Spanish versions of French poems written by Delfina Bunge de Gálvez. She is twenty-six, and it is the first time she is invited abroad to speak about another writer's work instead of reading her own. The venue is named in none of the chronologies, so the hall she stood in cannot now be identified. Montevideo will keep asking her over, and she will keep crossing.
suggested_refs: Delmira Agustini's Uruguayan reception, 1914-1919
Delfina Bunge de Gálvez, poems in French, in Storni's Spanish

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Irremediablemente
stops.date_confidence: CVC gives 1919 for the third collection without month or day; both are defaulted. The quotations were read off the digitized first edition. Coordinates are the generic Buenos Aires pin.
stops.campa: The third book comes out. She is twenty-six, three books in four years, with a job at the importer's, a teaching post, and a boy of seven at home. In this one stand the two poems Argentine schoolchildren will still be reciting a hundred years later. In the first, a woman tells a small man to open the cage and let the canary out, and adds that she is the canary. In the second, a man tells her that his father never wept, that his grandfather never wept, that the men of his blood were made of steel.
stops.quote: Hombre pequeñito, hombre pequeñito, / Suelta a tu canario que quiere volar... / Yo soy el canario, hombre pequeñito / Déjame saltar.
stops.quote_source: Hombre pequeñito..., in Irremediablemente (Buenos Aires, 1919), from the digitized first edition
suggested_refs: Irremediablemente (1919), first edition
Peso ancestral, in the same volume

stops.name: Buenos Aires, thirty-five pieces for La Nota
stops.date_confidence: Attested: emin_arslan.journey.json records the founding of La Nota on 14 August 1915 at 25 de Mayo 294, and Storni as a permanent contributor from 28 March to 21 November 1919 with thirty-five pieces, including Convalecer and Golondrinas; the research dossier gives the same dates independently. Coordinates are the corpus's generic Buenos Aires pin: the address at 25 de Mayo 294 was not geocoded.
stops.campa: From the twenty-eighth of March to the twenty-first of November she is a permanent contributor to La Nota, the weekly Emin Arslan founded in 1915 at 25 de Mayo 294: thirty-five pieces in eight months, Convalecer and Golondrinas among them, in a column given over to women's lives. Arslan prints her beside Lugones, Ingenieros, Ricardo Rojas, Alfredo Palacios, and Rubén Darío. Anthologies will keep her poems for seventy years and lose this prose entirely, until an editor goes back into the files in 2016 and finds it there.
suggested_refs: La Nota, Buenos Aires weekly, 1915-1921, and its Feminidades column
Un libro quemado (Editorial Excursiones, 2016), collecting her 1919-1921 articles from La Nota and La Nación
sources: argentina.gob.ar, 'Alfonsina Storni: 87 años de su fallecimiento'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the citizenship and the two prizes
stops.date_confidence: The citizenship date, 9 November 1919, is attested by CVC. The publication year of Languidez is contradicted between sources: CVC groups it under a November entry near the citizenship item, Spanish Wikipedia gives 1920, and 1920 is the more commonly cited year. The contradiction is not resolved; the two events are placed together here on the attested CVC date, which is an editorial decision and not a claim that they fell on the same day.
stops.campa: On the ninth of November the Swiss-born schoolteacher takes Argentine citizenship. She has lived in the country twenty-three of her twenty-seven years, and was carried into it at four by parents who had given up on Ticino. Languidez follows and carries off the First Municipal Poetry Prize and the Second National Literature Prize, which is as much as the state has to give a book of verse. The republic naturalizes her and decorates her inside a year. She goes on teaching, and goes on going in to the office in the morning.
suggested_refs: Languidez (1920), and the records of the First Municipal and Second National prizes

stops.name: Parque Chacabuco, the school for weak children
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC gives April 1921 for the post at the Escuela de Niños Débiles and 1923 for the creation of the chair of reading and declamation at the Escuela Normal de Lenguas Vivas. Neither carries a day. The Lenguas Vivas appointment is folded into this stop; its own coordinates would be -34.5992, -58.3892.
stops.campa: In April she takes a post at the Escuela de Niños Débiles in Parque Chacabuco, a public institution for undernourished children: weighing them, feeding them, teaching the ones the city's medicine has classified as weak. She is exhausted, anxious, and convinced she is developing tuberculosis. Two years later a chair of reading and declamation is created for her at the Escuela Normal de Lenguas Vivas. The girl who said other people's lines on a provincial stage is now paid to teach how a line is said.
suggested_refs: The Escuela de Niños Débiles, Parque Chacabuco, and Buenos Aires school hygiene in the 1920s
The chair of reading and declamation, Escuela Normal de Lenguas Vivas, created 1923

stops.name: Los Cocos, the sierra against the nerves
stops.date_confidence: CVC records annual rest stays at Los Cocos, in the Punilla valley of Córdoba, beginning in 1921, with no month or day; the date here is defaulted and orders the segment only. That José Ingenieros advised the stays is not in CVC, which records only that he was a close friend, and is carried as reconstruction. Coordinates from Nominatim for Los Cocos, departamento Punilla; an earlier working coordinate fell 27 km south near La Falda.
stops.campa: From this year she goes up every summer to Los Cocos, in the Punilla valley of Córdoba, where the air is dry and eight hundred kilometres keep Buenos Aires off. She rests there against nervous exhaustion and the depressions that come and go without warning her first. Ingenieros is a close friend in these years, and later accounts say it was he who sent her to the sierra. The chronology does not say that. It says only that she went, and that she kept going back.
suggested_refs: Los Cocos and the Punilla rest-cure circuit of the 1920s

segments.name: The Cellar, the Sea Festival, and the Three Performances

stops.name: Mar del Plata, the first Fiesta de la Poesía
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the date: CVC records that she organized and held the first Fiesta de la Poesía at Mar del Plata on 29 January 1925. CVC does not place it at La Perla. The coordinates are the Punta Iglesia end of the La Perla shoreline and stand for Mar del Plata generally, not for a documented festival site; earlier working coordinates for this town fell 2.5 km offshore.
stops.campa: She organizes and holds the first Fiesta de la Poesía at Mar del Plata on the twenty-ninth of January, having argued the thing into existence against a town with no use for it. Then she stands up in front of it and runs it. It is the first event on this coast that is hers rather than one she was invited to. The chronology gives the date and stops. What it does not give is who came: verse read out of doors, in a resort at the height of the season, to a crowd that came down for the water and the casino.
suggested_refs: The Fiesta de la Poesía, Mar del Plata, first held January 1925

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Ocre and the turn
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC gives May 1925 for Ocre and September 1926 for Poemas de amor, neither with a day. The quotation was read off the digitized 1925 second edition, Editorial Babel. Coordinates are the generic Buenos Aires pin. Poemas de amor is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: Ocre in May, and the register changes. The swooning has gone out of the verse; the irony is no longer decoration; she starts examining herself with the same eye she has been turning on men, and the self-portrait it produces is not flattering and is not meant to be. Sixteen months later Poemas de amor comes out, a cycle of short prose pieces, and pulls hard the other way. The two books sit a year apart in the bibliography and nobody has ever reconciled them. She is thirty-three.
stops.quote: Ten paciencia, mujer que eres oscura; / Algún día, la Forma Destructora / Que todo lo devora, / Borrará mi figura.
stops.quote_source: Humildad, in Ocre (Buenos Aires: Editorial Babel, 1925), from the digitized second edition
suggested_refs: Ocre (1925), Editorial Babel
Poemas de amor (1926), the prose-poem cycle

stops.name: Café Tortoni, the cellar of La Peña
stops.date_confidence: CVC places her in La Peña, the Agrupación Gente de Artes y Letras led by Benito Quinquela Martín in the Tortoni cellar, around 1926, with no month or day; both are defaulted. luis_perlotti.journey.json records the same table and states that no source it reached dates the gatherings. Two atlas files give slightly different Tortoni coordinates, -34.6086, -58.3773 and -34.6086, -58.3806; the first is used and the discrepancy is unresolved.
stops.campa: In the cellar of the Café Tortoni on Avenida de Mayo, Benito Quinquela Martín has gathered the Agrupación Gente de Artes y Letras and everyone calls it simply La Peña. She joins. At the same table sit Baldomero Fernández Moreno, Conrado Nalé Roxlo, Juana de Ibarbourou when she is over from Montevideo, and a young sculptor named Luis Perlotti who has made nothing anyone knows yet. Years after her death Perlotti will cut her profile into stone above the beach she drowns off, the garments blown back by a wind coming off the water.
suggested_refs: The Tortoni cellar and the Agrupación Gente de Artes y Letras
Luis Perlotti's stone relief of Storni facing playa La Perla, Mar del Plata, inscribed with lines from her 1925 poem Dolor
sources: buenosaires.gob.ar, 'Datos curiosos: escultura de Alfonsina Storni'

stops.name: Teatro Cervantes, three performances of El amo del mundo
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC gives the premiere on 10 March 1927 at the Teatro Cervantes, the original title Dos mujeres, and the closure after three performances. Coordinates geocoded to Av. Córdoba 1155; an earlier working coordinate sat 620 m off. That La debilidad de Mister Dougall, written 1927, went unstaged and was first published in the 2002 Losada prose volume comes from the bibliographic record and not from CVC.
stops.campa: Her three-act comedy opens at the Teatro Cervantes on the tenth of March under the title El amo del mundo, having been written as Dos mujeres. It sets a man's double standard up on a stage and lets two women take it apart in front of a paying audience, which is not what a Buenos Aires audience of 1927 has come out for. The press falls on it, on its treatment of women and on its treatment of men. She keeps writing plays, most of them for children; another written that same year is never staged and waits until 2002 to be printed. El amo del mundo closes after three performances.
suggested_refs: El amo del mundo (1927), and the press campaign against it
La debilidad de Mister Dougall (1927), first published 2002
sources: Delfina Muschietti, ed., Obras. Prosa: narraciones, periodismo, ensayo, teatro (Losada, 2002)

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the writers' society she built
stops.date_confidence: The 8 November 1928 inauguration of SADE under Leopoldo Lugones is attested in CVC, as is her organizing from October 1925 and her tenth-floor flat at Córdoba 807, whose address is confirmed by a 1927 letter held at the Museo de Coronda. The composition of the founding leadership, including Jorge Luis Borges, Horacio Quiroga, Manuel Gálvez and Roberto Giusti, comes from the research dossier; no atlas file documents that roster and it is carried as reconstruction. The Nosotros comment is undated in CVC and is adduced there for her role from October 1925.
stops.campa: Since October 1925 she has been convening meetings in her tenth-floor flat at Córdoba 807 to argue Argentine writers into a body that would defend them. It takes three years and, by the account printed at the time, a thousand difficulties. On the eighth of November the Sociedad Argentina de Escritores is formally constituted. Leopoldo Lugones presides over it; Horacio Quiroga, Manuel Gálvez, Roberto Giusti and Jorge Luis Borges are in the founding leadership. She is not given the top of it, and is not given it later either.
stops.quote: El animoso entusiasmo de una mujer, la ilustre poetisa Alfonsina Storni, ha logrado convertir en realidad, a través de mil dificultades, la vieja aspiración de agrupar los escritores argentinos en una sociedad que los ampare y defienda
stops.quote_source: Revista Nosotros, undated comment quoted in the Centro Virtual Cervantes chronology, adduced there as evidence that Storni was the first mover of what became SADE from October 1925
suggested_refs: Córdoba 807, Buenos Aires, tenth floor: the meetings of 1925-1928
The founding minutes of the Sociedad Argentina de Escritores, 8 November 1928
sources: Museo de Coronda, Storni letter of 1927 to Amelia Tuells (address record)

segments.name: Two Crossings and the Castelar Basement

stops.name: Madrid, the crossing with Blanca de la Vega
stops.date_confidence: Attested that CVC records the 1930 journey through Spain, France and Switzerland with Blanca de la Vega, and Diario de navegación in La Nación on 16 February 1930. No Spanish city is named in the sources consulted; Madrid is used as the likeliest node of the milieu she is said to have encountered and is not itself an attested stop. Month and day defaulted.
stops.campa: She sails for Europe with Blanca de la Vega and travels through Spain, France and Switzerland, standing for the first time since she was four in the country she was born in. She writes the voyage up as Diario de navegación and La Nación prints it on the sixteenth of February. The Spanish poets of the generation of 1927 are at work while she is there, a decade younger than she is and pulling their own language apart. Which of them she met, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: Diario de navegación, La Nación, 16 February 1930

stops.name: Hotel Castelar, the Signo basement and the Lugones charge
stops.date_confidence: Attested that CVC places both the start of her attendance at the Signo gatherings in the Hotel Castelar basement and the second European journey with her son in 1932, neither with a month or day; both defaulted. The quotation is verbatim from CVC's 1932 entry, where the two sentences form one continuous passage; the ellipsis is in CVC's own text and the passage runs on past where it is cut here.
stops.campa: She begins going down to the Signo gatherings in the basement of the Hotel Castelar on Avenida de Mayo. The same year she crosses to Europe a second time, taking Alejandro, twenty now, with her. And the same year she is accused of lifting a children's verse play out of Lugones, who presides over the society she spent three years building. Her answer is that she asked Lugones no permission, since she has no idea whom he asked first, and that the play is for her own pupils, the only people who believe she can write for a stage.
stops.quote: No le he pedido permiso a Lugones porque ignoro si él le pidió antes permiso a otro... Esta obra en verso es para teatro de niños y la destino a mis alumnos del teatro infantil que son los únicos que creen en mí como autor teatral.
stops.quote_source: Storni, 1932, defending Blanco... negro... blanco... against the charge that it copied Lugones's El pierrot negro; quoted as one continuous passage in the Centro Virtual Cervantes chronology (cronologia03.htm)
suggested_refs: Blanco... negro... blanco... and Lugones's El pierrot negro
The Signo group in the Hotel Castelar basement, Avenida de Mayo 1152

stops.name: Hotel Castelar, meeting García Lorca
stops.date_confidence: CVC's 1933 entry records the meeting with Federico García Lorca at the Signo gatherings in the Hotel Castelar; no month or day is given. federico_garcia_lorca.journey.json dates his Buenos Aires stay from October 1933 to March 1934, and the month here is taken from that file to order the segment. That file does not name Storni; the meeting rests on CVC.
stops.campa: Federico García Lorca comes to Buenos Aires in October and stays half a year, feted by a city that has decided he is the future of the language, and holds court in the same Castelar basement where Signo meets. He is thirty-five, inside what will turn out to be nearly all the life he gets. She is forty-one, a dozen books in, two years from finding the lump in her breast. That they met there is one line in the chronology, with no date on it, no witness, and no account of what was said.
suggested_refs: García Lorca's Buenos Aires season, October 1933 to March 1934, and the Castelar basement

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Mundo de siete pozos
stops.date_confidence: Attested to November 1934 by CVC, which records the dedication to her son Alejandro and the break toward irregular verse; no day is given. Coordinates are the generic Buenos Aires pin.
stops.campa: In November she publishes Mundo de siete pozos and dedicates it to Alejandro, who is twenty-two. The verse breaks open: irregular, unrhymed, built out of images that refuse to resolve, a human head described as a world with seven wells sunk into it. Apart from the dedication there is almost nothing in the book her readers recognize, and the ones who have been buying her since El dulce daño do not follow her there. She is forty-two, and she has written herself out of her own audience on purpose.
suggested_refs: Mundo de siete pozos (1934), dedicated to Alejandro Storni

segments.name: The Knife, the Notebook, the Sea

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the operation
stops.date_confidence: The date is attested by CVC and by Spanish Wikipedia, which names the sanatorio Arenales. The two records contradict on which breast: CVC gives the right, most derivative biographies give the left. The contradiction is not resolved. Coordinates are the generic Buenos Aires pin, CVC not naming the hospital.
stops.campa: On the twentieth of May, at forty-three, she goes under the knife for a malignant tumor of the breast and comes out of it without one. The Cervantes chronology records the right breast. Most of the biographies say the left. The surviving record does not settle it, and she is not asked. Everything she writes after this date is written by a woman who has been told what is in her body. She survives the operation and does not recover from the fact of it. She goes back to the classroom, to the newspapers, to the summer trips, to the letters.
suggested_refs: The sanatorio Arenales, Buenos Aires, and the surgical record of May 1935

stops.name: Mar del Plata, the town written as a film
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC gives Film marplatense in the Buenos Aires daily Crítica, February 1936, and describes it as a mixture of chronicle and prose poetry, quoting the passage used here. No day is given. Coordinates are the La Perla and Punta Iglesia shoreline standing for Mar del Plata; the piece was printed in Buenos Aires and written out of this town.
stops.campa: In February the daily Crítica prints Film marplatense, half chronicle and half prose poem, written out of the resort at the top of the season. The crowd on the beach, the crowd at the roulette table, the crowd on the rambla, all of it constantly palming its own faces away; the sea changing its skin minute by minute; the wave taking its victim and going off to digest it in the wet cellars underneath, with nobody watching. She has been coming to this town for eleven years.
stops.quote: No he venido a descubrir Mar del Plata. [...] El ambiente no da para más; la multitud, ya en la playa, ya en la ruleta, ya en la rambla, escamotea continuamente sus perfiles
stops.quote_source: Film marplatense, in the Buenos Aires daily Crítica, February 1936, quoted in the Centro Virtual Cervantes chronology; the bracketed ellipsis is in CVC's text and the sentence continues past the cut
suggested_refs: Film marplatense, Crítica, February 1936

stops.name: Santiago de Chile, the notebook at the train window
stops.date_confidence: Attested that CVC records a journey south through Argentina and into Chile in January 1937, the La Nación series Carné de ventanilla, and that she learned of Horacio Quiroga's suicide on returning in February. The route is not documented beyond Argentina and Chile: Santiago stands for the Chilean leg and is not an attested stop. Day and month defaulted.
stops.campa: In January she goes south and west, through Argentina and over into Chile, sending back the travel series Carné de ventanilla to La Nación: the notebook of a woman at a train window, twenty months out from the operation and still travelling. She comes home in February and learns that Horacio Quiroga, who stood with her at the founding of the writers' society nine years before, has killed himself. She writes about the trains and the cordillera and does not write about that.
suggested_refs: Carné de ventanilla, La Nación, 1937

stops.name: Montevideo, the platform with Mistral and Ibarbourou
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC gives 27 January 1938 for the shared Montevideo appearance with Gabriela Mistral and Juana de Ibarbourou, and gives the title of the conferencia she pronounced there, Entre un par de maletas a medio abrir y la manecilla del reloj. Earlier summaries calling that title a poem she read are wrong. The venue is not named in any source consulted; the coordinates are the Universidad de la República, the same unverified Montevideo point used for 1919.
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of January she shares a platform in Montevideo with Gabriela Mistral and Juana de Ibarbourou. Three women, three countries, one afternoon, and out of it comes the image of a triad that Spanish American anthologies will print for the rest of the century. What she gives is not a reading but a lecture, and its title sounds like a room half packed: between a pair of half-open suitcases and the hand of the clock. She has nine months left.
suggested_refs: Entre un par de maletas a medio abrir y la manecilla del reloj, Montevideo, 27 January 1938

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Mascarilla y trébol
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC gives August 1938 for the Espasa-Calpe Antología poética and September 1938 for Mascarilla y trébol: círculos imantados, neither with a day. Coordinates are the generic Buenos Aires pin. The Antología is folded into this stop.
stops.campa: In August the Espasa-Calpe Antología poética comes out, a working life gathered and priced. In September comes Mascarilla y trébol, subtitled círculos imantados: sonnets with the rhyme stripped out of them, which she calls antisonnets, images arriving unexplained and unapologized for and refusing to close. Two books in two months, one of them a summing up sold by a Spanish house and the other the least commercial thing she has ever set her name to. It is the most advanced writing she has done and it is the last book she publishes. She is forty-six.
suggested_refs: Mascarilla y trébol: círculos imantados (1938)
Antología poética (Espasa-Calpe, 1938)

stops.name: Estación Constitución, the train south
stops.date_confidence: Attested: CVC records the departure for Mar del Plata on 18 October 1938 and the posting of Voy a dormir to La Nación from there; the paper printed it on 25 October, the day of her death, and it also stands in Mascarilla y trébol. That Alejandro and Lidia Oriolo de Pizzigatti saw her off comes from the biographical record synthesized in the dossier and is corroborated in outline by CVC. The Spanish text quoted is from es.wikisource.
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of October she takes the train south from Constitución. Her son Alejandro sees her off on the platform, and Lidia Oriolo de Pizzigatti stands there with him. She has taken a room for the week. From Mar del Plata in the days that follow she posts La Nación a poem in which a woman asks a nurse made of flowers and dew to turn down the earthen sheets, and adds that if he telephones again he should be told not to insist, that she has gone out. The paper prints it on the twenty-fifth.
stops.quote: Dientes de flores, cofia de rocío, / manos de hierbas, tú, nodriza fina, / tenme prestas las sábanas terrosas / y el edredón de musgos escardados.
stops.quote_source: Voy a dormir, posted to La Nación from Mar del Plata in October 1938 and printed there on 25 October, the day of her death; also in Mascarilla y trébol. Spanish text from es.wikisource. The widely circulated English version carries no translator credit and could not be traced to a credited edition.
suggested_refs: Voy a dormir, La Nación, 25 October 1938

stops.name: Mar del Plata, the room on Tres de Febrero
stops.date_confidence: Attested in outline: CVC and the dossier record the lodging in the Oriolo family's establishment on Tres de Febrero, the letters of 19 and 22 October to Alejandro, and a final letter to Manuel Gálvez asking him to see that her son was looked after; a SADE manuscripts record is cited for the letters. The street number is not documented and the coordinates approximate Tres de Febrero in central Mar del Plata.
stops.campa: She takes a room in the Oriolo family's lodging house on Tres de Febrero, in the middle of town, a few blocks up from the water. She writes to Alejandro on the nineteenth and again on the twenty-second. She writes to Manuel Gálvez, the honorand of that Nosotros dinner twenty-two years back, at whose table she first sat down inside Argentine letters, and asks him to see that her son is looked after. Those letters and the poem she posts to La Nación are what survives of the week. Nothing else from those six days does.
suggested_refs: The Oriolo lodging on calle Tres de Febrero, Mar del Plata
The October 1938 letters to Alejandro Storni and to Manuel Gálvez
sources: SADE manuscripts repository record, cited in the research dossier

stops.name: La Perla, the espigón of the Club Argentino de Mujeres
stops.date_confidence: The date and the breakwater account are attested: argentina.gob.ar records that she threw herself from the espigón del Club Argentino de Mujeres at playa La Perla and that one of her shoes, caught in the ironwork, fixed the exact spot; CVC records the body recovered hours later and sent to Buenos Aires. The hour of about one in the morning comes from the dossier and is not confirmed. Coordinates are the Punta Iglesia end of La Perla; earlier working coordinates fell 2.5 km offshore. The image of a slow walk into the waves is reconstruction: English Wikipedia sets it against the biographers' breakwater account, and no eyewitness account exists in any source reached. Ariel Ramírez and Félix Luna's zamba Alfonsina y el mar fixed that image; the 1969 composition date, and the roles of Mercedes Sosa's and Chabuca Granda's recordings in spreading it, rest on the dossier alone.
stops.campa: About one in the morning she leaves the room and walks down to the breakwater of the Club Argentino de Mujeres at the south end of La Perla, and goes into the water. One of her shoes stays behind, caught in the ironwork of the espigón, and it is the shoe that tells anyone the exact place. The body is recovered hours later and sent up to Buenos Aires. Thirty-one years afterward a zamba will have her walking slowly into the waves until they close over her, and the country will learn it by heart. No witness ever saw that.
suggested_refs: The espigón del Club Argentino de Mujeres, playa La Perla, Mar del Plata
Ariel Ramírez and Félix Luna, Alfonsina y el mar, and the legend it fixed
sources: argentina.gob.ar, 'Alfonsina Storni: 87 años de su fallecimiento'

segments.name: The Two Graves and the Garden of Poets

stops.name: Recoleta, the vault that was not hers
stops.date_confidence: The wake at the Club Argentino de Mujeres in Buenos Aires and the first burial in the Botana and Medina Onrubia family vault at Recoleta are attested by CVC and Spanish Wikipedia. No burial day is given; 27 October orders the segment within the attested late-October window. The Senate homage of 21 November 1938 with Alfredo Palacios speaking is in the research dossier but could not be found in CVC cronologia01 to 03 or on any page reached, and is unverified.
stops.campa: The body is waked at the Club Argentino de Mujeres in Buenos Aires, an institution with the same name as the breakwater she went off. She is buried at Recoleta in the family vault of her friend Salvadora Medina Onrubia de Botana, who gives her a place among another family's dead, there being no Storni vault in this city or any other. The front pages carry it for days. On the twenty-first of November the Senate of the Republic holds a homage and Alfredo Palacios speaks.
suggested_refs: The Botana and Medina Onrubia vault, Cementerio de la Recoleta
Diario de sesiones del Senado de la Nación, 21 November 1938

stops.name: Chacarita, moved among the artists
stops.date_confidence: That her remains were transferred from the Recoleta vault to the artists' and public figures' sector of Chacarita is attested; Spanish Wikipedia confirms the present interment there. The date of 22 September 1963 is widely repeated in reference works but could not be confirmed on any page independently fetched during this research, and is carried as reconstruction. Coordinates from Nominatim for the Cementerio de la Chacarita; two research lenses returned conflicting pins and this is the harmonized value.
stops.campa: Twenty-five years after the burial her remains come out of the Botana vault and go across the city to Chacarita, into the ground the municipality keeps for artists and public figures. She gets a grave in her own name and her own right, having been lent one for a quarter of a century by a friend with a family vault to spare. By now the four lines about the small man and the canary are a schoolroom recitation piece. That the transfer happened is certain; the day of it, 22 September 1963, is repeated in every reference work and confirmed in none of them.
suggested_refs: The artists' sector of the Cementerio de la Chacarita, Buenos Aires
sources: luis_perlotti.journey.json (citing es.wikipedia for the Chacarita burial)

stops.name: Jardín de los Poetas, Palermo: the bust that could not be confirmed
stops.date_confidence: Undated. The date here is an ordering device only and carries no claim: the busts of the Jardín de los Poetas are not dated in any source reached, and Storni's presence among them is unconfirmed. Spanish Wikipedia's Rosedal de Palermo article gives twenty-six busts of poets and writers but names only nine in the retrievable portion, Storni not among them; the Buenos Aires municipal pages that would settle the roster returned 404 and connection errors. Coordinates are the canonical Jardín de los Poetas pin inherited byte-identical from jose_marti.journey.json and federico_garcia_lorca.journey.json; two other files in the corpus carry -34.575, -58.414 and -34.5706, -58.4173, a recorded and unresolved discrepancy.
stops.campa: In the Rosedal of Palermo, inside Parque Tres de Febrero, a garden of busts stands among the roses: poets and writers, twenty-six of them by the usual count, most of them of this hemisphere. Nine names can be read off the reachable lists and hers is not among the nine. The municipal registers that would settle the roster return errors. Whether the woman who came to this city at nineteen, pregnant and carrying Rubén Darío in her bag, has a face in the garden of poets is a question the record does not presently answer.
suggested_refs: The Jardín de los Poetas, El Rosedal, Parque Tres de Febrero, and its twenty-six busts
